summary: Describes the OPNFV VSPERF project's contributions to benchmarking virtual switches, mainly test setups and configuration parameters. It extends Benchmarking Methodology Working Group results to virtual switches on general-purpose hardware.

plainLanguage.summary: A test for how fast a software mail sorter works, written down so everyone runs it the same way.

subtitle: How to test virtual switches fairly and consistently on general-purpose hardware.

tldr.problem: Virtual switches for Network Function Virtualization lack clear benchmarking guidelines, making it difficult to compare performance fairly or reproduce results across different systems.
tldr.mechanism: The OPNFV project extends existing benchmarking methodology standards to virtual switches by defining detailed test setups, hardware/software configuration parameters, and deployment scenarios.
tldr.outcome: This RFC provides laboratories and vendors with repeatable benchmarking procedures for virtual switches, enabling consistent performance comparison.

today: RFC 8204 is an Informational RFC that documents OPNFV project work on virtual switch benchmarking. It remains a key reference for anyone implementing or testing virtual network functions. The benchmarking methodology continues to evolve as virtualization technologies advance.

sections.title: Virtual Switch Benchmarking Challenges
sections.content:
The Benchmarking Methodology Working Group (BMWG) has long tested dedicated physical network equipment in labs, measuring throughput, latency, and forwarding rates. But virtual switches running on general-purpose computers present new challenges: the same software switch performs differently depending on how the hardware is configured, what else is running on the computer, and how virtual machines are set up.

Virtual switches are essential to Network Function Virtualization (NFV), which aims to run telecom and networking functions as software instead of special hardware. This RFC extends BMWG standards to cover these virtualized implementations, drawing on the OPNFV VSPERF project, which focuses on real telecom workloads rather than just cloud computing scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: Virtual switches are pieces of software that move data between virtual and physical networks, but unlike physical switches, they can behave very differently depending on what hardware they run on.

sections.title: What Changes When Switches Are Virtual
sections.content:
Unlike a physical switch, a virtual switch competes for CPU cores, memory, and caches with other software. The RFC emphasizes comparing virtual and physical switches fairly requires identical benchmarks but also tracking how many CPU cores a virtual switch needs and how much memory it uses.

Configuration parameters become critical for reproducibility. The RFC lists over 50 specific hardware and software details that must be reported: BIOS version, power management settings, CPU microcode, memory type and frequency, hypervisor version, vSwitch version and parameters, virtual machine setup, and network interface configuration. Test traffic details also matter: duration, number of flows, packet sizes, and whether traffic uses UDP, TCP, or other protocols.

Flow classification affects results significantly. Virtual switches group packets into flows by matching header information. The RFC recommends classifying flows using input port, MAC addresses, IP addresses, and Ethernet type. The flow timeout must be increased before performance tests to avoid measuring the cost of installing new flows.
sections.plainLanguage: To test a virtual mail sorter, you need to write down everything: what computer it runs on, what software version, how many envelopes you send, what size they are, how long the test runs.

sections.title: VSPERF Test Specification
sections.content:
The VSPERF project builds on existing BMWG standards like RFC 2544 (Network Interconnect Devices) and RFC 2889 (LAN Switching). It adds tests for virtual switch scenarios including:

  • Throughput tests: Maximum forwarding rate in frames per second and megabits per second at zero loss.
  • Latency tests: Using IP Performance Metrics standards to measure delay distribution, percentiles, and outliers.
  • Scalability tests: Performance with increasing numbers of flows, ports, and forwarding rules.
  • Stream performance: How fast data transfers through the switch with TCP or UDP.
  • Control and data path coupling: How the switch's control plane affects data plane performance, especially the latency of the first packet in a flow.
  • Soak tests: Running for 24 hours or until instability appears to catch rare issues and memory leaks.

The specification also covers different deployment scenarios: traffic going through physical ports, through virtual machines, through chains of virtual machines, and from VMs back to physical ports.
sections.plainLanguage: You test how many postcards it can sort, how long each one takes, what happens when you sort thousands of different destinations, and whether it still works after running for a whole day.

sections.title: How Virtual Switches Are Deployed
sections.content:
Virtual switches operate in several different configurations, each presenting different performance characteristics:

Physical-to-Physical
Traffic enters one physical network port, passes through the vSwitch, and exits another physical port. This is the baseline scenario.
With Virtual Machines
Traffic passes through the vSwitch to a virtual machine, then through the vSwitch again to another physical port. The VM adds CPU overhead and latency.
Chained VMs
Multiple virtual machines are connected in series through the vSwitch, like a chain of processing steps.
VM to Physical
Traffic originates in a virtual machine and exits through a physical port, or vice versa.

Each scenario must be benchmarked with baseline measurements using isolated resources and progressively with more resources in use.
sections.plainLanguage: You test mail sorting in different situations: just at the mailroom, through a mail processing center, through several processing centers in a row.

sections.title: The 3x3 Matrix: What Gets Measured
sections.content:
VSPERF organizes tests into a matrix covering three lifecycle phases (Activation, Operation, De-activation) crossed with four qualities (Speed, Accuracy, Reliability, Scale). Activation means bringing a flow online; Operation is normal forwarding; De-activation is tearing down a flow.

Speed of Activation: How quickly the vSwitch learns a new destination and how fast the first packet arrives. Accuracy: Whether the control plane interactions (like adding a flow) actually result in the correct forwarding behavior. Reliability: Whether the switch recovers correctly from errors. Scale: How many addresses or flows the switch can handle.

The RFC describes the current coverage and identifies gaps, such as tests for De-activation and request/response performance, which are planned for future work.
sections.plainLanguage: For each part of the mail sorting process, you measure how fast, how accurate, how reliable, and how large a volume it can handle.
